h1:
Sisaket–Surin Cross-Province Trip
Tracing Thousand-Year Khmer Temples
intro: Sisaket and Surin sit right next to each other, and both are the real Khmer-temple heartland of lower Isan. If you've done just one province and still feel like you've left something on the table, plan to cross over to the other one in a single trip, because many of these temples line up along the same route, and an hour or so of driving puts a whole new set within reach. This article lays it out as a plan with a built-in schedule, starting with the temples on the Sisaket side, then crossing over to catch Surin's standouts like Sikhoraphum and Ban Phluang. There are 1-day, 2-day, and 3-day versions, so pick whatever fits the time you have.

blocks.html: Before we get to the schedule, here's the big picture on why a cross-province Sisaket–Surin plan makes sense. The key is that these two provinces border each other along Highway 226 and share the same northeastern rail line. Driving from downtown Sisaket to downtown Surin takes about 1–1.5 hours, and scattered along the way and around both towns are thousand-year-old Khmer temples. Plan the route well and you can hit the standout temples of both provinces in one trip without doubling back.

Let me be upfront: the plan in this article only includes temples that sit well inland and are open to visitors as usual. Surin's Ta Muen temple group, which sits right on the Thai–Cambodian border, is currently closed because of the border situation, so we've left it off the route and explain the details at the end of the article — including Pha Mo I Daeng and Khao Phra Wihan over on the Sisaket side.

blocks.text: Route overview: which temple is in which province

blocks.html: The idea behind this plan is to finish off the Sisaket-side temples first, since they cluster around Uthumphon Phisai and Huai Thap Than — right on the way toward Surin — and then keep driving across into Surin for the next set of standouts. Here are the main temples worth catching on this plan.

items: Sa Kamphaeng Yai (Sisaket · Uthumphon Phisai district) — the largest and most complete Khmer temple in Sisaket, about 26 km from the city, with three prangs, several lintels, and a temple museum. It's the highlight on the Sisaket side. Free entry.

Ban Prasat (Sisaket · Huai Thap Than district) — three brick prangs in the middle of a village inside Wat Prasat Phanaram, quiet and peaceful, sitting along the way before you cross into Surin. Free entry.

Sikhoraphum (Surin · Sikhoraphum district) — five brick towers on a single platform, known for the apsara and dvarapala carvings around the doorframe. It's the highlight on the Surin side. Open 7am–6pm, entry 10 THB for Thais.
Ban Phluang (Surin · Prasat district) — a single small white-sandstone sanctuary, but the carvings on its pediment and lintel are finely detailed and beautiful. Open 7am–6pm.

blocks.title: Sequence it so the drive flows without backtracking
blocks.html: If you're driving your own car, work from east to west: start with the Sisaket-side temples (Sa Kamphaeng Yai, then Ban Prasat), which lie along the way, then keep driving into Surin's Sikhoraphum district, which comes next on Highway 226. From there, head south to Ban Phluang in Prasat district. This route runs one direction the whole way — no doubling back.

blocks.text: If you only have 1 day: catch the highlight of each province

blocks.html: If you've only got a single day but want both provinces, this plan focuses on one highlight temple per side — Sa Kamphaeng Yai in Sisaket and Sikhoraphum in Surin — then slots in a smaller temple along the way if there's time. Leaving a little earlier in the morning makes it most comfortable.

blocks.label: Single Day
blocks.title: Sa Kamphaeng Yai, then over to Sikhoraphum

items.activity: Leave downtown Sisaket, drive along Highway 226 toward Uthumphon Phisai
items.note: Fuel up and grab water in town first — convenience stores in the villages are limited

items.activity: Sa Kamphaeng Yai, the Sisaket highlight: walk the three prangs, lintels, and temple museum
items.note: Allow about an hour. Free entry

items.activity: Drive on toward Huai Thap Than and stop at Ban Prasat, brick prangs in the middle of a village
items.note: About 20–30 min. Skip it if you're short on time

items.activity: Lunch along the way into Surin, around Sikhoraphum
items.note: Isan restaurants and rice-and-curry spots in the district town, easy on the wallet

items.activity: Sikhoraphum, the Surin highlight: see the five towers and the apsara carvings
items.note: Open 7am–6pm, entry 10 THB for Thais, walk it in about 45–60 min

items.activity: If you still have energy, head south to Ban Phluang in Prasat district for the pediment carvings
items.note: Small temple but finely detailed carvings, about 30 min to walk

items.activity: Head into downtown Surin, find dinner before driving back or staying over
items.note: If returning to Sisaket, it's about an hour's drive

blocks.title: One day is a bit packed
blocks.html: The one-day plan does cover everything, but you'll drive a lot and have little time to spare. If you can swing it, stretch it to 2 days, 1 night for a much more relaxed trip — you get to stay a night in Surin and don't have to rush the drive back in the evening.

blocks.text: 2 days, 1 night: stay one night in Surin

blocks.html: This is our favorite version. Day one, take your time with the Sisaket-side temples, then drive over to sleep in Surin. Day two, catch the Surin temples and the local food of the elephant town before heading back. You get it all — temples, food, and a stay in each city.

blocks.text: 3 days, 2 nights: go deep on both provinces

blocks.html: If you're set on a full temple-hunting trip, three days is just right. Day one, do the Sisaket temples plus a temple in town. Day two, cross to Surin for Sikhoraphum, Ban Phluang, and the elephant town. Day three, catch the secondary temples and the souvenirs of both provinces before heading home.

blocks.text: Which temple is most worth it if you have to cut some

blocks.html: If you don't have time to hit them all, here's how we'd rank them for value, looking at the temples of both provinces together. Use it to decide what to cut.

items.name: Sikhoraphum (Surin)
items.blurb: Five brick towers on a single platform, known for the apsara and dvarapala carvings around the entrance doorframe. It's the prettiest and most photogenic temple on the route. If you can only pick one on the Surin side, pick this.

items.name: Sa Kamphaeng Yai (Sisaket)
items.blurb: The largest and most complete in Sisaket, with three prangs and several lintels — including Indra on his elephant and Vishnu reclining on the cosmic serpent — plus a temple museum showing excavated finds. If you can only pick one on the Sisaket side, pick this.
items.meta: Uthumphon Phisai district · 26 km from city · 45–60 min

items.name: Ban Phluang (Surin)
items.blurb: A single small white-sandstone sanctuary, but the pediment and lintel carvings are finely detailed and very beautiful — great for anyone who likes studying the craftsmanship up close. It's south of Surin city.
items.price: Small entry fee, check on site

items.name: Ban Prasat (Sisaket)
items.blurb: Three brick prangs in the middle of a village inside a temple, quiet, with few crowds — you get the feel of a temple still living alongside its community. It's along the way before you cross into Surin, so it's an easy stop.
items.meta: Huai Thap Than district · on the way · 20–40 min

items.name: Sa Kamphaeng Noi (Sisaket)
items.blurb: A Khmer arogayasala (hospital) by the roadside with a pond in front of the sanctuary. Less remains than at the others, but it sits right on the main road, so it's a quick stop along the way.
items.meta: Uthumphon Phisai district · roadside on Hwy 226 · 20–30 min

blocks.text: Food and souvenirs from both provinces

blocks.html: Temple-hopping is tiring, so you'll want some food to cap it off. Both Sisaket and Surin are Isan towns with good food, and each has its own kind of souvenirs — pick some up before you head home from either one.

items.name: Food on the Sisaket side
items.blurb: Local Isan food, khanom chin with curry sauce, rice congee for breakfast, and the grilled-pork hotpots in the evening where locals meet up. Top souvenirs are shallots, garlic, jasmine rice, and seasonal volcanic-soil durian (Jun–Aug).

items.name: Food on the Surin side
items.blurb: Khmer-style grilled pork eaten with dipping sauce, bold Isan dishes, and Vietnamese kuay chap in town. The signature souvenirs are handwoven village silk in old patterns and Surin jasmine rice.

blocks.title: Make temple visits more fun
blocks.html: Read a little about Khmer art before you go, then watch for what the lintels and pediments are telling — it's more fun than just standing around taking photos. Go in the morning or late afternoon when the sun is low; you'll see the depth of the carvings far better than under flat midday light, especially the apsara figures at Sikhoraphum.

blocks.text: Prep before setting out on the cross-province route

items: Transport — your own car or a rental is by far the easiest. The temples are spread across the outer districts of both provinces and public transport reaches them only with difficulty. If you arrive by train or bus into the city, rent a car or hire a driver for the day.
Main route — use Highway 226 as the spine linking Sisaket–Uthumphon Phisai–Sikhoraphum–Surin. It runs one direction smoothly, and most temples are not far off this road.

Best time — the cool season (November–February) has good weather, so walking the temples under the sun isn't punishing. In the rainy season the temples turn lush and green but the ground gets slippery.
What to wear — comfortable walking shoes and a sun hat, since the temples are out in the open with little shade.

Costs — the Sisaket-side temples are free; the Surin side has small entry fees (Sikhoraphum is 10 THB for Thais). Your main costs are fuel, lodging, and food — it's a history trip that's easy on the budget.

blocks.text: The border temples to avoid right now

blocks.html: To be clear: Surin's most famous Khmer temples — the Ta Muen group (Ta Muen Thom, Ta Muen Toht, Ta Muen) — sit right along the Thai–Cambodian border in Phanom Dong Rak district. There have been violent clashes in this area recently, so the 2nd Army Region ordered Ta Muen Thom and Ta Kwai closed, strung barbed wire, and still has troops deployed even after a ceasefire agreement. For that reason we don't put the Ta Muen group on this plan and recommend avoiding it for now.

The Sisaket side is the same. Pha Mo I Daeng and Khao Phra Wihan National Park in Kantharalak district also sit on the border. The park announced a temporary closure of Pha Mo I Daeng from late May 2025, with no firm reopening date.

blocks.title: Check every time before you set out
blocks.html: Before even thinking about going near Ta Muen, Pha Mo I Daeng, or Khao Phra Wihan, always check the announcements from the 2nd Army Region and Khao Phra Wihan National Park, plus the latest border news. If it's still closed or unsafe, skip it and visit only the inland temples on this plan instead. The Sa Kamphaeng Yai–Ban Prasat–Sikhoraphum–Ban Phluang route is all well inland, nowhere near the border, and open as usual.

faq.q: How many days do you need for a Sisaket–Surin cross-province plan?
faq.a: If you only catch the highlight temple on each side — Sa Kamphaeng Yai in Sisaket and Sikhoraphum in Surin — a single day works but it's packed and you'll drive a lot. For a relaxed trip with a night in Surin, 2 days, 1 night is the sweet spot. And if you mean to do the secondary temples and the food of both cities in full, 3 days, 2 nights fits best.

faq.q: How far is it from downtown Sisaket to downtown Surin?
faq.a: About 1–1.5 hours by car along Highway 226, the main road linking the two provinces through Uthumphon Phisai and Sikhoraphum. Many Khmer temples are not far off this road, which makes it work nicely as a single-trip temple trail across the two provinces.

faq.q: What are Sikhoraphum's opening hours and entry fee?
faq.a: Sikhoraphum, in Sikhoraphum district of Surin province, is open for visits roughly 7am–6pm daily. Entry is 10 THB for Thais and 50 THB for foreigners. Its standout features are the five brick towers on a single platform and the apsara and dvarapala carvings around the doorframe — it's the most photogenic temple on this route.

faq.q: Do you need your own car to visit the temples across both provinces?
faq.a: Pretty much, yes. The temples are spread across the outer districts of both Sisaket and Surin, and public transport reaches them only with difficulty. If you arrive by train or bus into the city, rent a car or hire a driver for the day — that's the smoothest way to work through the temples across the provinces.

faq.q: Can you go to Ta Muen Thom in Surin?
faq.a: Not recommended right now. The Ta Muen group (Ta Muen Thom, Ta Kwai) sits on the Thai–Cambodian border in Phanom Dong Rak district. There have been violent clashes recently, and the 2nd Army Region ordered it closed and strung barbed wire — troops remain deployed even after a ceasefire agreement. Always check the army's announcements and the latest border news before going. That's why the plan in this article picks only inland temples like Sikhoraphum and Ban Phluang instead.
